enonce_markdown: A Biology teacher shows an animation of blood circulation with a video projector. Which benefit of ICT in education does this mainly illustrate?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Match the example with the benefit it provides: multimedia -> visualisation; Internet -> access to resources; software -> practice and feedback.

### Solution

An animation makes a hidden, moving process visible, so it supports **understanding of abstract concepts through visualisation**. The projector does not mark essays, change furniture costs or remove the need to take notes.

choix.texte: Learners can visualise processes that cannot be observed directly
A reduced need for learners to take notes

enonce_markdown: (a) Define the term *e-learning*. (b) State **two** advantages of e-learning for a student living in a village far from a good school.
A school has 30 computers, but the public electricity supply is available only about 3 hours per day, so the computer room is rarely usable. Which measure deals most directly with this barrier?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Identify the barrier first (here power supply), then choose the measure that removes that barrier rather than one that improves something else.

### Solution

The problem is the **lack of a reliable electricity supply**. Solar panels with batteries provide power throughout the day. Larger monitors, antivirus software and wireless keyboards do not change the amount of electricity available.

choix.texte: Buy larger monitors for the computers
Install more antivirus software on each computer
Install solar panels with batteries to supply the computer room
Replace the keyboards with wireless keyboards

enonce_markdown: A teacher uploads recorded video lessons and posts forum tasks. Learners watch the videos and answer the tasks at any time during the week, with no live session. What type of e-learning is this?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Synchronous learning takes place live at the same time; asynchronous learning allows learners to take part at different times.

### Solution

The learners are not required to be online together: they choose when to watch and reply, so it is **asynchronous**. Synchronous e-learning would need a live class (for example video conference at a fixed time). Face-to-face teaching needs a physical class, and computer-based testing is about assessment, not about delivering lessons.

enonce_markdown: A school has 600 students and one computer room with 40 computers. The room is open 40 hours per week. (a) How many students share each computer? (b) Assuming the room is always fully used, what is the average number of computer hours per student per week (to 1 decimal place)? (c) Suggest two ways of improving access.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Divide the number of students by the number of computers for the sharing ratio; divide the total computer-hours available by the students for the access time.

### Solution

**(a)** $600 \div 40 = 15$ students per computer.

**(b)** Computer-hours available per week: $40 \times 40 = 1600$. Per student: $1600 \div 600 \approx 2.7$ hours per week.

**(c)** Any two: open the room in the evening and at weekends; add computers or tablets; set up a timetable so that classes use the room in turns; use projects done in groups; install a solar power supply and Internet access to make better use of the existing machines.

enonce_markdown: A newspaper claims that giving every learner a tablet will automatically raise exam results. Which evaluation is the most accurate?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

To evaluate a claim, look for the conditions on which the result depends rather than accepting an absolute statement.

### Solution

Devices are only a tool. Benefits depend on how teachers are trained to use them, on relevant digital content, on power and connectivity and on integration into teaching. The word *automatically* makes the claim too strong, and the opposite claim that ICT can never help is equally too strong. A tablet does not replace the teacher's role of guiding learning.

choix.texte: True: any ICT device motivates learners, so results rise whatever the use
False: ICT devices can never have a positive effect on learning
True: tablets store textbooks, so the teacher is no longer needed for results to improve
Not necessarily: the effect depends on teacher training, suitable content, connectivity and how the tablets are used in lessons
